comments.text:
"Money is debt" is the stupidest mistake the economists ever made.
Yes, you can implement your monetary policy like that and you will get a financial pyramid (a ponzi scheme of sorts) that is guaranteed to blow up in your face after some time. That is asinine, and if done on purpose, quite malicious.
We see today that cryptocurrency (as ridiculous as it is) can function as currency (from an economic theory point of view). Therefore the money doesn't have to be created through debt. We have a very important piece of empirical evidence, yet we parrot that 2019 line and worship the fake gods of MMT.
Money has to be separated into two logical entities: (1) the theoretical measurement system (measurement of what you may ask, measurement of desirability) and (2) the physical or electronic currency tokens which can be exchanged for goods and services (the store of value system). When you say that a banana costs 1 dollarbuck you use the measurement system. When you pay 1 dollarbuck for a banana, you use money in the capacity of store of value. System (1) is theoretically unlimited, like when Musk claims that SpaceX is worth more than the combined economy of Earth. System (2) is limited to issued currency tokens (all physical cash and valid records of bank deposits).
Once you think of money as this dual logical entity that is separate yet intertwined, the statement that money is debt starts to look more like a engineering proposition, rather than an economic principle.

replies.author: @jeancarrenpao
replies.text:
Actually, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) says otherwise.

BIS explicitly explains that banks create transaction deposits when they extend loans and destroy those deposits when the loans are repaid.

You're describing what banks may do afterward with their lending activities. But issuing a new loan is another act of money creation. It does not mean the money extinguished through the previous loan repayment magically remained in circulation.

You're confusing two separate accounting events: money destruction through repayment and money creation through new lending.

Even BIS recognizes that distinction.

Official source: BIS, Unpacking International Banks' Deposit Funding (2023)

replies.author: @jeancarrenpao
replies.text:
​@deansmash7844You're confusing the recycling of credit with the creation and extinguishment of money.

When a borrower repays the principal, the bank reduces its loan asset and extinguishes the corresponding deposit liability. That money is removed from circulation. It does not automatically become a new deposit for another client.

If the bank subsequently issues another loan, it creates a new deposit through a new credit transaction. That's a separate act of money creation, not proof that the original repayment money was never extinguished.

The distinction matters: repayment is money extinguishment. New lending is money creation. One does not cancel out the accounting reality of the other.

replies.author: @deansmash7844
replies.text: ​@jeancarrenpao Unfortunately that's not how it actually plays out in a fractional reserve system. Every deposit,. including "repayments" gets 10% held in reserve and the bank will issue another set of loans and credits to the next client

comments.text:
Look, according to recent statistics there's 11 trillion USD on the planet, and 102 trillion in outstanding debts (private and public).  Suppose I'm Elon Musk and I take out a loan for a 1 trillion dollar house.  When I do that, I create a trillion dollars of money and a trillion dollars of debt.  There's now 12 trillion USD on the planet, and 103 trillion debts.  Over the course of the next 30 years I make several hundred payments to the bank, for a total of two trillion dollars because I'm paying back the interest and the principal.  At that point, the amount of debt in the world is back to where it was before I took out the loan (102 T).  But the USD available on the planet isn't 11 trillion again - it's now 10 trillion.  

However, I'm not the only actor in this economy, and other people are taking out loans all the time.  In fact without the influx of new money from new loans we'd quickly run out of all available cash in a few years.  But every loan has interest, and every time interest is paid the ratio between total debts and total available money gets worse and worse.

It wasn't always like this.  We didn't always have a debt based society.  Before the federal reserve we used to have a society based on capital - gold, and silver.  We say we're capitalist but the truth is we haven't been a capitalist society for a long time.
